title: Meta's enterprise AI platform rattles software stocks, MongoDB shares
excerpt: The poaching of MongoDB's CEO highlights Meta's push to turn its fast-growing AI ambitions into a major enterprise business.
content_html:
Another week. Another move from Meta that flips the AI trade upside down.

Last week, Meta's agentic-AI push minted new winners in the chipmaking space and sent its own shares up sharply, cementing the company as a frontrunner in consumer AI.

But CEO Mark Zuckerberg doesn't seem content to stop there — he also wants to disrupt enterprise software. Meta made the bold move of poaching MongoDB president and CEO CJ Desai right before the company's investor day, appointing him to run the new enterprise platform.

MongoDB got crushed, falling 18% on the day. Perhaps more surprising was that Meta fell 5%. Investors may be weighing the risk of pursuing consumer and enterprise AI at once, although profit-taking after a huge post-Muse rally was likely also a factor.

The more consequential moves came in software. Investors quickly began repricing a familiar fear: Meta's arrival could further threaten incumbents already under pressure, although losses did ease as the day progressed.

It turns out Zuck had another ace up his sleeve all along, and Muse was just one part of the master plan. The question now is how it will balance both initiatives — and convince investors that each is on track.

Ambitions beyond consumer AI

The Muse push made a ton of sense to investors because Meta already has a massive built-in audience across its multiple apps. If they can convert even a sliver of those people into Muse users, the upside is immense.

Breaking into enterprise software and convincing clients to use Meta AI for their businesses is another matter entirely. The company needs credibility if people are going to use its tech stack throughout their operations.

That's where Desai comes in. He's someone with existing relationships that can get people to start using Meta software and, most importantly, stick with it long term.

Software isn't one trade anymore

So what does this mean for the market? Monday's stock recovery in the space shows it's not as simple as "software go down." This isn't SaaSpocalypse 2.0. There's some nuance to the winners and losers.

The software companies most at risk are those whose products handle repetitive tasks: workflow tools, customer-service platforms, and developer software. If Meta's agents can do more of that work directly, those companies could lose pricing power.

The most defensible area may be the firms that make agents usable: data-management providers like Snowflake, plus cybersecurity companies such as CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks. Meta can build the interface, but it still needs help connecting it safely to a business's systems.

Ultimately, Meta is trying to own both ends of the AI boom. And, as usual, investors are pricing outcomes on the fly. Expect more volatility across the space as other gigantic companies unveil their own transformational ambitions.
